text:
### Observed differences

- The relative order of two groups of activities reversed. Before, A20 came before A15, A17 and A18 in all 200 before-traces, and whichever of A14, A16 or A19 ran came before A20 and before A24; in the later window, A15, A17 and A18 come before A20 in all 200 after-traces, and A14/A16/A19 come after A20 and after A24. Every measured cross-pair between the two groups flipped its order in essentially all traces (for example, A20 preceded A15 in 200 of 200 before-traces and follows it in 200 of 200 after-traces). [REL008, REL015, REL018, REL004, REL012, REL020, REL005, REL009]
- Event positions moved accordingly: A15, A17 and A18 shifted from a mean position of about 64% of the trace to about 38%, while A14, A16 and A19 shifted from about 34–35% to about 67–68%; A20 (about 38% to 44%) and A24 (about 57% to 64%) moved slightly later. [POS002, POS004, POS005, POS001, POS003, POS006, POS007, POS008]
- Routing around the two groups swapped. A14, A16 and A19 always led to A20 before and always lead to A25 in the later window; the exits of A15, A17 and A18 that previously went to A25 (roughly 30–38% of their observed outgoing transitions each) now go to A20 (roughly 28–37%), with A25 no longer observed among their outgoing transitions. A24's observed successors changed from A15/A18/A17 to A19/A16/A14, and A35's from A16/A14/A19 to A17/A15/A18. [DIR001, DIR003, DIR006, DIR002, DIR004, DIR005, DIR007, DIR008]
- Distances changed consistently with a three-activity block and a one-activity block exchanging places: the gap from A24 to A25 shrank from 4 to 2 event positions, and the gap from A35 to A20 grew from 2 to 4. [LAG001, LAG002]
- Participation was essentially stable: A15, A17, A18, A20 and A24 appear in every case in both windows, and A14, A16 and A19 each appear in roughly 29–39 in 100 cases in both windows, their shares summing to about one occurrence per case. [POS001, POS003, POS006, POS002, POS004, POS005, POS007, POS008]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that two segments of the process exchanged their order: the segment in which A15, A17 and A18 all run (previously exiting to A25) and the segment in which one of A14, A16 or A19 runs (previously exiting to A20) swapped places around A20, A24 and A35. Before, traces ran A35, one of A14/A16/A19, A20, A24, then A15/A17/A18 and A25; in the later window they run A35, A15/A17/A18, A20, A24, then one of A14/A16/A19 and A25. [REL008, REL015, REL018, DIR001, DIR002, DIR007, DIR008, LAG001, LAG002]

The support is direct and consistent: 39 qualifying items against roughly 0.46 expected if nothing had changed is far beyond what an unchanged process typically produces; every item's difference exceeds about 995 of 1,000 random re-splits of the pooled data; the order reversals are near-complete rather than marginal; and the successor, position and distance changes all fit one quantitative story — each gap shifts by exactly the two-position size difference between a three-activity block and a one-activity block. These items largely re-describe a single underlying difference, so they should be read as one coherent signal rather than independent confirmations. [DIR001, POS002, REL008, LAG001, LAG002]

A competing explanation the two-window design cannot rule out is a shift in the mix of pre-existing variants: if both orderings already existed and their frequencies flipped between the windows (for example from nearly all one ordering to nearly all the other), the same signatures would appear without any structural modification. The small participation changes for A14, A16 and A19 (about 29–39 in 100 cases) could likewise be sampling noise or a minor routing change, and the position and distance indicators use event positions, not clock time, so no timing claim is implied. [POS001, POS003, POS006, POS002, POS004, POS005]
